claims.text: PL 117-263 sec. 1673 carries the statutory note '50 USC 3373b'; enacted title 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA REPORTING PROCEDURES'; 136 Stat. 2959-2962. Approved 23 December 2022.

Sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) covers 'any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

Sec. 1673(b)(1)(A)-(C): an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement', 'shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526 ... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2271 et seq.)', and 'is not a violation of section 798 of title 18, United States Code'.

Sec. 1673(a)(4)(A) requires sharing of an authorized disclosure with AARO personnel 'regardless of the classification of information contained in the disclosure or any nondisclosure agreements', unless the disclosure likely relates to a SAP or compartmented access program already 'explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees, and is documented as meeting those criteria.'

Sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) legislates a reporting channel for programmes involving 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development' relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.
Sec. 1673(b)(1)(A) provides that an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure.'
Sec. 1673(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal including revocation or suspension of security clearances or termination of employment.

Sec. 1673(b)(3)(A) requires agencies and contractors to conduct comprehensive searches of all records relating to nondisclosure orders on these subjects and to provide copies to AARO for congressional access.

desc: Section 1673 is the provision that makes the legacy programme a matter of enacted federal law rather than allegation, and it is routinely underrated. It orders the Secretary of Defense, through the head of AARO, to establish a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of 'any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.' Congress does not legislate reporting channels for categories of programme it believes do not exist. The protections are unusually strong: an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure,' is deemed to comply with Executive Order 13526 and with chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act, and 'is not a violation of section 798 of title 18' or any other disclosure statute. Reprisal — including 'the revocation or suspension of security clearances, or termination of employment' — is prohibited. Subsection (b)(3) then orders DoD, ODNI, DHS, other supporting agencies and Federal contractors that 'have supported or are supporting such activities and programs' to conduct comprehensive searches of all records relating to nondisclosure orders on these subjects and deliver copies to AARO, which must make them accessible to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership. This is a statutory census of the gag orders. It has never been reported as completed.
